title: Client reactions and biases in PMS
objectives: Respond to three common PMS client statements.
Keep the focus on portfolio-level results.
body_md:
| Client says | Bias behind it | Respond with |
|---|---|---|
| "This stock is down 40%, tell the manager to sell it." | Loss aversion, illusion of control | "You're paying the manager for the whole portfolio. Let's judge the portfolio against its benchmark, not one stock." |
| "My friend's PMS made 60% last year. Let's move." | Recency, herd | "Let's compare both on after-fee returns over five years, including their worst year." |
| "The market is up but my PMS isn't." | Short-term framing | "This style lags in some phases. Here's how it did across a full cycle." |

> **Investor takeaway:** Higher potential returns come with bigger dips. Staying the course matters even more in PMS.
example: A client says, 'This stock is down 40%, tell the manager to sell it.' You explain that the manager is judged on the whole portfolio against its benchmark, not on one stock.
say: Let's compare both on after-fee returns over five years, including their worst year.
This style lags in some phases. Here's how it did across a full cycle.
never: Yes, tell the manager to sell it.
Your friend's PMS is clearly better.

check.q: "This stock is down 40%, tell the manager to sell it." Which bias?
o: Loss aversion and illusion of control
check.why: Respond: you pay the manager for the whole portfolio; judge it against its benchmark, not one stock.

check.q: "My friend's PMS made 60% last year. Let's move." Best response?
o: Switch immediately to capture the gains
Compare both on after-fee returns over 5 years, including their worst year
Tell the client their friend is lying
Promise the current PMS will do better next year
check.why: This is recency and herd behaviour.

check.q: 'The market is up but my PMS isn't.' What is the best framing?
o: This style lags in some phases; look at a full cycle
check.why: Short-term framing hides how a style performs across a full cycle.
